docs.title: Ayyappaswamy Eethakota
docs.text:
Linux Systems Administrator and High-Performance Computing (HPC) Engineer with hands-on experience supporting large-scale, production-grade HPC environments for government and enterprise research workloads.

This site documents my professional experience, technical skills, and operational knowledge gained while working on multi-petaflop HPC infrastructure, GPU-accelerated clusters, high-speed InfiniBand networks, and enterprise Linux systems.

docs.title: Professional Overview
docs.text:
I support and operate large-scale Linux and HPC environments used for mission-critical research and engineering workloads. My responsibilities include cluster administration, job scheduling, monitoring, automation, and incident management across CPU and GPU-based systems.

I have contributed to the deployment and sustained operation of India’s multi-petaflops HPC infrastructure, supporting environments with over 1,300+ compute nodes and NVIDIA H100 GPU accelerators.

docs.title: Areas of Work
docs.text:
Linux System Administration: Managing and maintaining Linux systems across many computers, ensuring they run smoothly, are secure, and are kept up-to-date.

HPC Cluster Management: Setting up and managing large clusters of computers used for high-performance computing (HPC), using tools like Bright Cluster Manager.

Workload Scheduling and Management: Using job schedulers such as PBS Pro and Slurm to manage and schedule tasks on the system, ensuring tasks run efficiently without delays or failures.

PBS Pro Job Scheduling and Management: Configuring and managing PBS Pro for job scheduling in high-performance computing environments, including creating job queues, monitoring job execution, troubleshooting job failures, optimizing resource allocation, and ensuring efficient workload distribution across compute nodes.

Hardware Troubleshooting: Identifying and fixing hardware issues like CPU failures, memory problems, network card faults, and other hardware-related issues in large systems.

Software Installation and Configuration: Installing both commercial and open-source software applications, configuring them correctly, and troubleshooting any issues that arise, including job scheduling problems.

Network Management: Ensuring that all computers in the cluster can communicate properly with each other, setting up InfiniBand networks, and solving any network-related issues.

System Monitoring and Performance Tuning: Monitoring the performance of systems and clusters, identifying areas that can be improved, and applying solutions to increase system performance and reliability.

Security Management: Applying security measures like firewalls, access controls, and system updates to keep the system secure from unauthorized access and attacks.

Automation and Scripting: Writing simple scripts to automate tasks like software installation, system checks, and data backups, making processes faster and more efficient.

Lustre File System Management and Troubleshooting: Managing and maintaining the Lustre File System to ensure high-performance storage across multiple nodes, including setting up, troubleshooting issues, tuning performance, and ensuring data integrity and accessibility.

Mellanox UFM (Unified Fabric Manager) Monitoring: Setting up and managing Mellanox UFM to monitor and manage high-speed InfiniBand networks in HPC environments, ensuring optimal network performance, diagnosing and resolving network-related issues, and maintaining fabric health across multiple nodes and switches.

Dell OpenManage Enterprise (OME) Management: Managing Dell OpenManage Enterprise (OME) to monitor and manage server health, perform firmware updates, and troubleshoot hardware issues in a large-scale environment, ensuring the stability and performance of Dell servers across the data center.

HPL Benchmarking and Performance Tuning: Running and analyzing HPL (High Performance Linpack) benchmarks to evaluate the performance of HPC systems, identifying bottlenecks, and fine-tuning system configurations to maximize computational efficiency and achieve optimal performance in scientific and engineering workloads.

24×7 Production Support and Incident Management: Providing continuous L2 support for production systems, including monitoring system health, diagnosing and resolving hardware and software issues, managing incidents, and ensuring minimal downtime in mission-critical environments.

docs.title: Deploy MkDocs Material Website to GitHub Pages (Step-by-Step)
docs.text: This document explains how to deploy an MkDocs Material website to GitHub Pages using the repository:

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure the following are installed on your system:

git --version
mkdocs --version

If MkDocs Material is not installed:

pip install mkdocs-material

docs.title: 2. Project Structure (Expected)
docs.text:
Your project directory should look like this:

Material/
├── docs/
│   ├── index.md
│   ├── assets/
│   │   └── Ayyappaswamy_Resume.pdf
│   └── ...
├── mkdocs.yml
└── .gitignore

Note: MkDocs only uses files inside the docs/ directory.

docs.title: 3. Navigate to Project Directory
docs.text: cd ~/Material

docs.title: 4. Initialize Git Repository
docs.text:
If Git is not initialized yet:

git init

Add the GitHub remote repository:

git remote add origin https://github.com/hpcteam/hpcteam.github.io.git

Verify:

git remote -v

docs.title: 5. Create .gitignore File (Important)
docs.text:
Create a .gitignore file to avoid committing generated files:

cat <<EOF > .gitignore
site/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
EOF

docs.title: 6. Commit Source Files
docs.text:
Add all files:

git add .

Commit:

git commit -m "Initial MkDocs Material website"

Rename branch to main and push:

git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

docs.title: 7. Deploy to GitHub Pages Using MkDocs
docs.text:
MkDocs provides a built-in deployment command.

Run:

mkdocs gh-deploy

This will:

  • Build the site
  • Create a gh-pages branch
  • Push static files automatically

docs.title: 8. Enable GitHub Pages (One-Time Setup)
docs.text:
1. Open GitHub repository: hpcteam/hpcteam.github.io
  2. Go to Settings → Pages

  3. Under Source:

  4. Branch: gh-pages

  5. Folder: / (root)
  6. Click Save

Wait 1–2 minutes for deployment.

docs.title: 9. Access the Live Website
docs.text:
Your site will be available at:

https://hpcteam.github.io

docs.title: 10. Updating the Website (Regular Workflow)
docs.text:
Whenever you modify content:

git add .
git commit -m "Updated documentation"
git push
mkdocs gh-deploy

docs.title: Site Not Loading
docs.text:
• Wait a few minutes
  • Verify GitHub Pages branch is gh-pages

docs.title: Theme or CSS Missing
docs.text:
pip install --upgrade mkdocs-material
mkdocs gh-deploy --force

docs.title: 404 Errors
docs.text:
• Ensure filenames match exactly (case-sensitive)
  • Verify paths in mkdocs.yml

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
• main branch → source files
  • gh-pages branch → deployed website
  • mkdocs gh-deploy handles everything automatically

docs.title: What is query_other_jobs?
docs.text:
In PBS (Portable Batch System), the query_other_jobs option determines whether users can see the jobs that other users have submitted to the system.

  • Default Setting: True (Enabled by default)

Possible Values:

  • True — Users can see jobs submitted by other users.
  • False — Users can only see their own jobs.

docs.title: What Happens When query_other_jobs is Enabled (True)?
docs.text:
When query_other_jobs is set to True, users have the ability to view jobs that have been submitted by other users. This enhances transparency and coordination.

  • Job Visibility: All users can see each other's jobs.
  • Transparency: Users can check the status of any job on the system, even if they didn’t submit it.
  • Collaboration: It’s easier for users to coordinate and manage resources, especially in shared environments where multiple users are utilizing the same resources.

docs.title: What Happens When query_other_jobs is Disabled (False)?
docs.text:
When query_other_jobs is set to False, job visibility is limited to only the user's own jobs. This ensures privacy but limits transparency.

  • Job Visibility: Users can only see their own jobs, not those submitted by others.
  • Privacy: Job details are kept private between users, so no one can see what others are working on.
  • Limited Collaboration: Users can’t check the status of other users' jobs, making it harder to coordinate resources in a multi-user environment.

docs.title: How to Set query_other_jobs to False
docs.text:
To disable this feature, run the following command:

qmgr -c "set server query_other_jobs = False"

docs.title: When Should You Enable query_other_jobs?
docs.text:
You should enable query_other_jobs in environments where users need to:

  • Coordinate job statuses in a shared or collaborative environment.
  • Increase transparency so users can see each other’s job progress, helping to manage system resources more effectively.
  • Avoid conflicts by ensuring users know what jobs are running and if resources are being over-utilized.

docs.title: When Should You Disable query_other_jobs?
docs.text:
You should disable query_other_jobs when:

  • Privacy is a priority and you want to ensure that job details are only visible to the user who submitted them.
  • Security-sensitive systems where job-related information should not be shared between users.
  • Isolated environments where users don’t need to view the status of others’ jobs for coordination or resource management.

docs.title: Creating and Configuring a Local Repository in RHEL (Without Subscription)
docs.text: This guide explains how to create and configure a local YUM/DNF repository on RHEL systems without an active Red Hat subscription. The repository can be created using downloaded RPMs or RHEL ISO images.

docs.title: 1. Install Required Dependencies
docs.text:
Install the required tool to generate repository metadata:

dnf install -y createrepo

docs.title: 2. Obtain Repository Packages
docs.text: You can obtain RPM packages in two ways:

docs.title: Option 1: Download Packages Using reposync
docs.text:
If the system has temporary internet access:

reposync --reponame=<repository-name> -p /local-repo

Example:

reposync --reponame=baseos -p /local-repo

docs.title: Option 2: Use RHEL DVD ISO Images (Offline Method)
docs.text: If you have RHEL ISO images (recommended for offline environments), you can configure the local repository using those images.

docs.title: 3. Create Directory Structure for Local Repositories
docs.text:
Create directories to store RPM files:

mkdir -p /local-repo/baseos
mkdir -p /local-repo/appstream
mkdir -p /local-repo/highavailability

docs.title: 4. Copy RPM Files to Local Repository
4.1 Copy from External Media (USB / Mounted Disk)
docs.text:
If the RPMs are already available on external media:

rsync -avz /run/media/<user>/RHEL/BaseOS/* /local-repo/baseos
rsync -avz /run/media/<user>/RHEL/AppStream/* /local-repo/appstream
rsync -avz /run/media/<user>/RHEL/HighAvailability/* /local-repo/highavailability

docs.title: 4.2 Copy from RHEL ISO Image
docs.text:
Mount the RHEL ISO image:

mkdir -p /mnt/iso_image
mount rhel9.4.iso /mnt/iso_image

Verify contents:

ls -l /mnt/iso_image

You should see directories such as BaseOS and AppStream.

Copy the RPMs:

rsync -avz /mnt/iso_image/BaseOS/* /local-repo/baseos
rsync -avz /mnt/iso_image/AppStream/* /local-repo/appstream

⚠️ Note The HighAvailability repository is not included in standard RHEL ISO images. It must be downloaded separately if required.

docs.title: 5. Create Repository Metadata
docs.text:
Generate metadata so dnf can recognize the repositories:

createrepo /local-repo/baseos
createrepo /local-repo/appstream
createrepo /local-repo/highavailability

⚠️ If errors occur, verify that RPM files were copied correctly.

docs.title: 6. Configure Local Repository Files
docs.text:
Create a repository configuration file:

vi /etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo

Add the following content:

[local-baseos]
name=Local BaseOS Repository
baseurl=file:///local-repo/baseos
enabled=1
gpgcheck=0

[local-appstream]
name=Local AppStream Repository
baseurl=file:///local-repo/appstream
enabled=1
gpgcheck=0

[local-highavailability]
name=Local HighAvailability Repository
baseurl=file:///local-repo/highavailability
enabled=1
gpgcheck=0

🔹 gpgcheck=0 is recommended for offline/local repositories. If GPG keys are available, you may enable it.

docs.title: 7. Verify Repository Configuration
docs.text:
Check whether repositories are enabled:

dnf repolist

or

yum repolist

docs.title: 8. Clean DNF Cache
docs.text:
Clear existing cache and reload metadata:

dnf clean all
dnf makecache

docs.title: 9. Install Packages from Local Repository
docs.text:
Example: Install pcs package:

dnf install pcs

docs.title: 10. Verify PCS Installation
docs.text:
Check whether the service is installed and running:

systemctl status pcsd

Check available commands:

pcs --help

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Configuring a local repository in RHEL without a subscription allows systems to operate fully in offline or restricted environments. Using ISO images or synced RPMs ensures consistent package availability and simplifies system management.

docs.title: What is LVM?
docs.text:
LVM (Logical Volume Manager) is a storage management system in Linux that adds an abstraction layer between physical storage devices and filesystems.

Its main purpose is to make disk storage:

  • Flexible
  • Expandable
  • Easier to manage

Instead of working directly with fixed disk partitions, LVM allows administrators to work with logical storage units that can be resized and reorganized easily.

docs.title: Why LVM Is Needed
docs.text:
Traditional disk partitioning has limitations:

  • Partitions have fixed sizes
  • Expanding storage often requires downtime
  • Adding new disks is difficult
  • Disk space cannot be easily shared

LVM overcomes these limitations by separating:

  • Physical storage from
  • Logical storage

This separation allows dynamic storage management.

docs.title: LVM Storage Layers
docs.text:
LVM is built using multiple logical layers. Each layer has a specific role.

Physical Disk → Physical Volume → Volume Group → Logical Volume → Filesystem → Mount Point

docs.title: 1. Physical Disk
docs.text:
A physical disk is a real storage device such as:

  • Hard disk
  • SSD
  • Virtual disk

It provides raw storage capacity but has no understanding of files or directories.

docs.title: 2. Partition (Optional Layer)
docs.text:
A partition is a defined section of a physical disk.

Although LVM can work directly on entire disks, partitions are often used for:

  • Organization
  • Compatibility
  • Disk layout clarity

Partitions act as containers that can later be managed by LVM.

docs.title: 3. Physical Volume (PV)
docs.text:
A Physical Volume (PV) is a disk or partition that has been initialized for use by LVM.

When a PV is created:

  • LVM writes metadata on it
  • The space is divided into equal-sized blocks called Physical Extents

A PV is the basic building block of LVM.

docs.title: 4. Volume Group (VG)
docs.text:
A Volume Group (VG) is a storage pool created by combining one or more Physical Volumes.

Key characteristics:

  • Aggregates total storage capacity
  • Can grow by adding more PVs
  • Acts as a single large storage unit

The VG hides the complexity of multiple disks.

docs.title: 5. Logical Volume (LV)
docs.text:
A Logical Volume (LV) is a virtual storage unit created from a Volume Group.

Characteristics:

  • Acts like a traditional disk partition
  • Can be resized
  • Can span multiple physical disks
  • Used to store filesystems

Logical Volumes are the main objects users interact with in LVM.

docs.title: 6. Filesystem
docs.text:
A filesystem defines how data is stored and organized on a Logical Volume.

Responsibilities:

  • Manages files and directories
  • Handles permissions and metadata
  • Controls space allocation

Common filesystems include ext4 and XFS.

docs.title: 7. Mount Point
docs.text:
A mount point is a directory in the Linux filesystem hierarchy where a filesystem is attached.

Once mounted:

  • Data on the Logical Volume becomes accessible
  • The filesystem integrates into the system’s directory tree

docs.title: Extents
docs.text:
• Physical Extents (PE): Fixed-size blocks on a Physical Volume
  • Logical Extents (LE): Mapped blocks used by Logical Volumes

LVM maps LEs to PEs dynamically, enabling flexibility and resizing.

docs.title: Key Advantages of LVM
docs.text:
• Dynamic resizing of storage
  • Ability to add disks without downtime
  • Improved storage utilization
  • Support for snapshots
  • Better abstraction of physical hardware

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• LVM separates physical storage from logical usage
  • Storage is managed in layers
  • Logical Volumes provide flexibility over traditional partitions
  • Filesystems operate on LVM, not directly on disks

docs.title: Create and Mount an LVM Volume on a New Disk
Attach a Virtual Disk to Your Hyper-V VM
docs.text:
1. Shut down the VM.
  2. Open Hyper-V Manager.
  3. Right-click on the VM and select Settings.
  4. Under Hardware, select SCSI Controller (or add one if it's not there already).
  5. Click Add > Hard Drive > New.
  6. Choose VHDX or VHD, set the size for the new virtual disk, and click OK.
  7. Start the VM.

docs.title: 1. Verify the New Disk
docs.text:
Check if the new disk is visible to the system:

lsblk
fdisk -l

Example output:

sdb       8:16   0  100G  0 disk

docs.title: 2. Create a New Partition
docs.text:
Use fdisk to create a Linux partition on /dev/sdb:

fdisk /dev/sdb

Inside fdisk, perform the following: - Press n → create a new partition - Press p → primary partition - Accept defaults for sector unless specific sector sizes are needed - Define size, e.g.: +95G - Press w → write changes and exit

Verify the new partition:

fdisk -l /dev/sdb

You should now have /dev/sdb1.

docs.title: 3. Create a Physical Volume (PV)
docs.text:
pvcreate /dev/sdb1

Confirm:

pvs
pvsdisplay

docs.title: 4. Create a Volume Group (VG)
docs.text:
vgcreate earth_volume_group /dev/sdb1

Check VG details:

vgdisplay

docs.title: 5. Create a Logical Volume (LV)
docs.text:
Allocate 90 GB for the new logical volume:

lvcreate -L 90G -n my_logical_volume earth_volume_group

List LVs:

lvs

Confirm LV path:

/dev/earth_volume_group/my_logical_volume

docs.title: 6. Create a Filesystem on the LV
docs.text:
Format the logical volume with the ext4 filesystem:

mkfs.ext4 /dev/earth_volume_group/my_logical_volume

docs.title: 7. Create a Mount Directory
docs.text: mkdir -p /HOME

docs.title: 8. Mount the New Filesystem
docs.text: mount /dev/earth_volume_group/my_logical_volume /HOME

docs.title: 9. Verify the Mount
docs.text:
df -Th

Expected output:

/dev/mapper/earth_volume_group-my_logical_volume  ext4  89G   24K  84G  1% /HOME

docs.title: 10. Make the Mount Persistent
docs.text:
Before editing /etc/fstab, always back it up:

cp /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.bak

Get the UUID of the newly formatted LV:

blkid /dev/earth_volume_group/my_logical_volume

Example output:

/dev/earth_volume_group/my_logical_volume: UUID="6a62873b-95f8-4252-b73d-82daa7378b11" TYPE="ext4"

Copy the UUID shown for the device. Edit /etc/fstab:

vi /etc/fstab

Add this line at the end (replace <UUID> with the actual UUID):

UUID=<UUID>  /HOME  ext4  defaults  0  0

docs.title: 11. Test the fstab Entry
docs.text:
Unmount and remount to ensure the entry works:

umount /HOME
mount -a
df -Th

You should see /HOME mounted automatically.

docs.title: LVM Structure Diagram
docs.text:
[Physical Disk: /dev/sdb]
          │
          ▼
[Partition: /dev/sdb1] ← we have to create
          │
          ▼
[Physical Volume (PV): /dev/sdb1] ← we have to create
          │
          ▼
[Volume Group (VG): earth_volume_group] ← we have to create
          │
          ▼
[Logical Volume (LV): my_logical_volume] ← we have to create
          │
          ▼
[Filesystem: ext4]
          │
          ▼
[Mount Point: /HOME]

docs.title: LVM Components Summary
docs.text:
• Physical Disk: The entire disk device.
  • Partition: Disk section created with fdisk, e.g., /dev/sdb1.
  • Physical Volume (PV): LVM-initialized partition, e.g., after pvcreate /dev/sdb1.
  • Volume Group (VG): Pool of storage created by combining PV(s), e.g., earth_volume_group.
  • Logical Volume (LV): Virtual disk partition allocated from VG, e.g., my_logical_volume.
  • Filesystem: Format the LV with a filesystem like ext4.
  • Mount Point: Directory to access the data, e.g., /HOME. ```

docs.title: What is Lustre?
docs.text:
Lustre is a high-performance, distributed (parallel) file system mainly used in:

  • HPC clusters (scientific simulations, CFD, weather, AI/ML)
  • Supercomputers
  • Large research data centers
  • GPU clusters and big data workloads
  • Compute nodes do the calculations
  • Lustre stores and serves data to all nodes at very high speed
  • Many nodes can read/write the same file at the same time

NOTE: Lustre separates file information (metadata) from file data to achieve very high performance.

docs.title: Main Components and Their Roles
docs.text: Term Meaning MDS Metadata Server (file info only) MDT Metadata Target (disk for metadata) OSS Object Storage Server OST Object Storage Target (data disks) Client Compute node using Lustre Striping Splitting a file across many OSTs Object A chunk of a file LNET Network layer used by Lustre Parallel I/O Many nodes read/write simultaneously

docs.title: 🧠 Metadata Server (MDS)
docs.text:
• Stores file information only
  • File name, permissions, owner, size, directory structure
  • Does NOT store file data

docs.title: 💾 Object Storage Servers (OSS)
docs.text:
• Store the actual file data
  • Each file is split into chunks (objects)
  • These chunks are stored across multiple OSS nodes

docs.title: 📦 Object Storage Targets (OST)
docs.text:
• Disks or disk groups attached to OSS
  • Actual location of data blocks

docs.title: 💻 Clients (Compute Nodes)
docs.text:
• Nodes that read/write data
  • Ask MDS for metadata
  • Read/write data directly to OSS

docs.title: MDS (Metadata Server)
docs.text:
MDS (Metadata Server) is like the librarian of the Lustre file system.

  • It does NOT store the file data
  • It only stores information ABOUT files

That information is called metadata.

docs.title: What is metadata?
docs.text:
Metadata means:

  • File name
  • Folder (directory) name
  • Who owns the file
  • Who is allowed to read/write
  • Where the file’s data is stored

This metadata is saved on a disk called MDT (Metadata Target).

docs.title: 1. Client → MDS
docs.text:
The client sends a metadata request to the Metadata Server (MDS), such as:

  • Create file
  • Open file
  • Stat / lookup
  • Permission check

docs.title: 2. MDS → MDT
docs.text: The MDS forwards the request to the Metadata Target (MDT), asking: “Do you have the metadata for this file?”

docs.title: 3. MDT (Metadata Storage)
docs.text:
The MDT is where metadata is actually stored. It contains:

  • File name
  • Directory hierarchy information
  • Permissions (mode bits / ACLs)
  • Owner and group
  • Timestamps (atime, mtime, ctime)
  • File layout information (e.g., OST striping info)

docs.title: 4. MDT → MDS (Response)
docs.text:
The MDT responds to the MDS with one of the following:

  • For read / lookup operations:
  • Returns the requested metadata
  • For create / delete / update operations:
  • Confirms that the metadata was successfully modified

docs.title: 5. MDS (Processing)
docs.text:
After receiving the response, the MDS:

  • Verifies permissions
  • Applies or manages metadata locks
  • Coordinates consistency
  • Prepares the final response

docs.title: 6. MDS → Client
docs.text: The MDS sends the result back to the client (success, failure, or metadata info).

docs.title: What is OSS?
docs.text:
OSS = Object Storage Server

  • OSS is a server (machine)
  • Its job is to serve file data to clients

Think of OSS as: A data server that handles read/write requests

An OSS can manage multiple OSTs.

docs.title: What is OST?
docs.text:
OST = Object Storage Target

  • OST is the actual storage (disk or filesystem)
  • This is where the file data is stored

Think of OST as: A hard disk (or storage unit) that holds file blocks

docs.title: Relationship
docs.text:
OSS (server)
├── OST1 (disk/storage)
├── OST2 (disk/storage)
└── OST3 (disk/storage)
  • OSS = controls access
  • OST = stores data

docs.title: How OSS and OST Work Together
1. Client wants to read/write a file
docs.text:
Example:


cp file1 /lustre

docs.title: 2. Client asks MDS (not OSS yet)
docs.text:
• “Where is this file stored?”

MDS replies:

  • “Your file is on OST1 and OST2”

docs.title: 3. Client talks directly to OSS
docs.text:
• Client sends data request to the OSS
  • OSS knows:
  • Which OST has which part of the file

docs.title: 4. OSS accesses the OST
docs.text: • OSS reads/writes data on the OST disks

docs.title: 5. Data flows back to client
docs.text:
Client ⇄ OSS ⇄ OST

(OSS is the middle manager for the disks)

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• Many OSS servers
  • Many OST disks
  • Many clients working at the same time

This allows:

  • Parallel data access
  • High speed I/O

docs.title: One-Line Definitions
docs.text:
• OSS: Server that handles file data requests
  • OST: Storage where actual file data lives

docs.title: Client and Data Flow Summary
docs.text: In Lustre, the client contacts the MDS only for metadata and then communicates directly with OSS/OST for actual data I/O.

docs.title: “Client talks directly to OSS/OST” — what it really means
docs.text: The client gets file info from MDS, but gets file data from OSS/OST.

docs.title: Real-life analogy 🏬
docs.text:
• MDS = Reception desk
  • OSS/OST = Warehouse

  • Client = Customer

  • You ask the reception desk (MDS): “Where is my package stored?”

  • Reception says: “Your package is in Warehouse A, Shelf 3”
  • You go directly to the warehouse (OSS/OST)
  • You take the package yourself

👉 Reception never touches the package

docs.title: 1. Client opens a file
docs.text:
vi data.txt
  • Client asks MDS:
  • Does file exist?
  • Do I have permission?
  • Where is the data stored?

docs.title: 2. MDS replies with layout
docs.text: MDS says: “The data is on OST1 and OST2”

docs.title: 3. Client talks directly to OSS/OST
docs.text:
• Client sends read/write requests straight to OSS
  • Data flows:

Client ⇄ OSS/OST

❌ MDS is not involved in data transfer

docs.title: 1. What is a Cluster
docs.text: A cluster is a group of computers (nodes) that work together. Many users share the same system, so software versions must be managed carefully.

docs.title: 2. What is a Module in a Cluster?
docs.text:
A module is an easy way to load, unload, and switch software environments. Instead of installing software separately for each user, the cluster provides: - Multiple versions of software (Python, GCC, CUDA, MPI, etc.) - Users choose what they need using modules

Think of a module like a switch: - “Turn ON Python 3.10” - “Turn OFF Python 3.8”

docs.title: 3. What Problem Do Modules Solve?
docs.text:
Without modules: - Software versions conflict - Environment variables get messy - One version breaks another

With modules: - Clean environments - Multiple versions coexist - Easy to change setups

docs.title: 4. What is a Module File?
docs.text:
A module file is a small configuration file that tells the system: - Where the software is installed - What environment variables to set

It usually: - Updates PATH - Sets LD_LIBRARY_PATH - Sets variables like PYTHONPATH, CUDA_HOME, etc.

📁 Example location:

/usr/share/modules/modulefiles/
/opt/modulefiles/

docs.title: 5. What Does a Module File Do?
docs.text:
When you run:

module load python/3.10

The module file:

  • Adds Python 3.10 binaries to your PATH
  • Makes sure libraries are found
  • Hides other Python versions

When you unload it:

module unload python/3.10

Everything is cleaned up.

docs.title: 6. Very Important Module Commands
docs.text:
module avail        # See available modules
module load xyz     # Load a module
module unload xyz   # Unload a module
module list         # See loaded modules
module purge        # Unload everything

docs.title: 7. Simple Analogy 🧠
docs.text:
• Cluster → shared kitchen
  • Software → ingredients
  • Module → choosing which ingredient set you’re allowed to use
  • Module file → recipe that tells the kitchen where everything is

docs.title: 8. Typical Examples of Modules
docs.text:
• gcc/11.2
  • python/3.9
  • openmpi/4.1
  • cuda/12.0

Each one has its own module file.

docs.title: 9. Before Creating a Module File
docs.text:
You need two things:

  1. Software already installed somewhere
  2. Permission to write module files (or do it in your own directory)

📌 Example software install:

/opt/apps/myapp/1.0/
├── bin/
├── lib/
└── include/

docs.title: 10. Decide Module Name & Location
docs.text:
Module files are usually stored like:

/opt/modulefiles/myapp/1.0

If you don’t have admin access, you can use:

$HOME/modulefiles/myapp/1.0

docs.title: 11. Tell the System Where Your Modulefiles Are
docs.text:
(Only needed for personal modules)

module use $HOME/modulefiles

docs.title: 12. Create the Module File
docs.text:
Create the file:

mkdir -p $HOME/modulefiles/myapp
vi $HOME/modulefiles/myapp/1.0

docs.title: 13. Basic Module File (Tcl Format)
docs.text:
This is the simplest working module file.

#%Module1.0
##
## myapp 1.0 module file
##

proc ModulesHelp { } {
    puts stderr "Loads myapp version 1.0"
}

module-whatis "MyApp version 1.0"

# Set base directory
set root /opt/apps/myapp/1.0

# Update environment
prepend-path PATH $root/bin
prepend-path LD_LIBRARY_PATH $root/lib

docs.title: 14. Load and Test the Module
docs.text:
module avail myapp
module load myapp/1.0
which myapp

If it works 🎉 you’re done.

docs.title: 15. Unload Test
docs.text:
module unload myapp/1.0

Your PATH should go back to normal.

docs.title: 16. Important Common Commands Inside Module Files
docs.text:
Command What it Does set Define variables prepend-path Add path at the beginning of a variable append-path Add path at the end of a variable setenv Create environment variable conflict Prevent version clashes

Example:

conflict myapp
setenv MYAPP_HOME $root

docs.title: 17. Common Mistakes 🚨
docs.text:
• Wrong install path
  • Forgetting module use
  • Using append-path instead of prepend-path
  • Not handling version conflicts

docs.title: 18. What Is Inside the Module File?
%Module1.0
docs.text: • Required header: Tells the module system: “This file is a module file.” Without this line, the module will not load.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text: • For humans only. Helps document what this module is for. It has no effect on execution.

docs.title: proc ModulesHelp { }
docs.text:
• Defines a help procedure: proc = procedure (function in Tcl)
  • ModulesHelp is a special name recognized by the module system.
  • This runs when the user types:

bash module help myapp/1.0

docs.title: module-whatis
docs.text:
• Short description: Displayed when the user runs:

bash module avail

It provides a one-line summary of the module.

docs.title: Set Base Directory
docs.text:
set root /opt/apps/myapp/1.0
  • Defines a variable: Assigns a value to a variable (root is the variable name, /opt/apps/myapp/1.0 is the installation directory).

docs.title: Update Environment
docs.text:
prepend-path PATH $root/bin
prepend-path LD_LIBRARY_PATH $root/lib
  • Modifies PATH: Adds /opt/apps/myapp/1.0/bin to the beginning of PATH.
  • Ensures this version is found before others.
  • $root is the value of the variable defined earlier.

docs.title: Result of Loading the Module
docs.text:
When you run:

module load myapp/1.0
  • The myapp command becomes available.
  • Correct libraries are found.
  • The environment is cleanly modified.

When you unload it:

module unload myapp/1.0
  • All changes are reversed automatically.

docs.title: What is NFS?
docs.text: The NFS (Network File System) is a file system protocol that allows you to access files over a network as if they were stored locally on your own machine.Port 2049 This is the default port for NFS itself (both TCP and UDP).

docs.title: Basic Understanding:
docs.text:
1. Purpose: NFS allows computers to share files and directories across a network. For example, a file stored on one computer can be accessed and edited by another computer in the same network, even though the file is physically located on the first computer.

  2. How it Works:

  3. A NFS server shares specific directories or files over the network.
  4. A NFS client can then mount the shared file systems and access them as though they are part of the local file system.

This happens using the NFS protocol, which defines how file access requests are made and how the server responds.

key advantages of using NFS (Network File System):

docs.title: 1. Centralized File Management:
docs.text: • NFS allows you to centralize file storage on a single server, making it easier to manage, back up, and secure files. Users can access these files across multiple systems without needing local copies.

docs.title: 2. Cross-Platform Compatibility:
docs.text: • NFS is supported by a variety of operating systems, including Linux, Unix, Mac OS, and even Windows (via third-party software). This makes it a versatile solution for environments with mixed OSes.

docs.title: 3. Seamless File Sharing:
docs.text: • NFS allows remote systems to access files over a network as though they are local. This creates a seamless user experience, where networked file access is similar to working on files stored locally.

docs.title: 4. Ease of Setup:
docs.text: • Setting up NFS is straightforward and does not require much configuration. Once the NFS server is set up and the shared directories are exported, clients can easily mount them, often with a single command.

docs.title: 5. Efficient Performance:
docs.text: • NFS is highly efficient for accessing and transferring files across a network. It supports caching and file locking mechanisms, making it a fast and

docs.title: Basic NFS Example:
docs.text:
1. On the server: The NFS server shares a directory.
   sudo exportfs /shared/folder

2.On the client: The client mounts the shared directory.

sudo mount -t nfs server_ip:/shared/folder /mnt

docs.title: Step 1: Install Required Packages on Server Node
docs.text:
Install the required NFS and rpcbind packages on the server.

sudo yum install nfs-utils rpcbind

Check the status of the NFS server.

systemctl status nfs-server

If it's not running, restart the service.

systemctl restart nfs-server

docs.title: Step 2: Check the Firewall Service
docs.text:
Check the status of the firewall.

systemctl status firewalld.service

Stop the firewall if it's not required.

systemctl stop firewalld.service

Alternatively, if the firewall service must remain enabled, add the necessary services and enable the required port numbers.

docs.title: Step 3: Create the Directory to Share Across the Network
docs.text:
Create the directory that you want to share.

mkdir /directory_which_is_to_be_shared

Change the ownership of the directory.

chown nfsnobody:nfsnobody /directory_which_is_to_be_shared

If necessary, change the directory permissions.

chmod 755 /directory_which_is_to_be_shared

docs.title: Step 4: Add Shared Directory Information in /etc/exports
docs.text:
Edit the /etc/exports file to add the directories you wish to share.

/directory_which_is_to_be_shared ip_address_of_network(rw,sync,no_root_squash)
/directory_which_is_to_be_shared ip_address_of_client_machine(rw,sync,no_root_squash)

docs.title: Step 5: Verify Export Values
docs.text:
Check and verify the export values with the following commands:

exportfs -a
exportfs -r
exportfs -v

Everything is good! Now we need to configure the NFS client.

docs.title: Step 6: Check Network Connectivity to the NFS Server
docs.text:
Ensure the network is reachable from the NFS client machine to the NFS server.

You can use the ping command to check connectivity.

ping ip_address_of_nfs_server

Check the firewall rules and enable the required ports if necessary.

docs.title: Step 7: Create a Mount Directory
docs.text:
Create the directory where the NFS share will be mounted on the client machine.

mkdir /mnt/nfs_mount

docs.title: Step 8: Mount the NFS Share
docs.text:
Mount the NFS share from the server to the client.

mount ip_address_of_nfs_server:/directory_which_is_to_be_shared /mnt/nfs_mount

docs.title: Step 9: Permanent Mount After Reboot
docs.text:
To make the NFS mount persistent across reboots, add the NFS server details in the /etc/fstab file.

Edit /etc/fstab and add the following line:

ip_address_of_nfs_server:/directory_which_is_to_be_shared /mnt/nfs_mount nfs defaults 0 0

docs.title: Step 10: Verify the Mount
docs.text:
Check if the NFS mount is successful.

mount | grep nfs

Alternatively, use the df -h command to verify the mounted file systems.

df -h

docs.title: What is pip?
docs.text:
pip stands for Pip Installs Packages and is the default package manager for Python. It allows you to install, upgrade, and manage Python libraries and packages that are available in the Python Package Index (PyPI).

Here’s a quick overview of what pip does:

  • Install Packages: You can use pip to install Python packages from PyPI or from a local directory.
  • Upgrade Packages: You can upgrade installed packages to their latest versions.
  • Uninstall Packages: You can remove unwanted packages from your Python environment.
  • List Packages: You can list all the installed packages in your Python environment.

docs.title: Basic Commands:
docs.text:
1. Install a Package:

To install a package from PyPI:

pip install package_name

Example:

pip install numpy
  1. Upgrade a Package:

To upgrade an existing package to the latest version:

pip install --upgrade package_name

Example:

pip install --upgrade numpy
  1. Uninstall a Package:

To remove an installed package:

pip uninstall package_name

Example:

pip uninstall numpy
  1. List Installed Packages:

To list all the installed packages:

pip list
  1. Check Package Version:

To check the version of a specific package:

pip show package_name

Example:

pip show numpy

docs.title: Step 1: Download Python Packages on the Internet-Connected Machine
a. Create a requirements.txt File
docs.text:
If you know which packages you want to install, create a requirements.txt file. For example:

numpy
pandas
matplotlib

docs.title: b. Download Packages and Dependencies Using pip
docs.text:
On an internet-connected machine, use pip to download the packages and their dependencies:

mkdir ~/offline_pkgs

pip download -r requirements.txt -d ~/offline_pkgs

This command will download all the necessary .whl (wheel) files and dependencies into the ~/offline_pkgs directory.

if you want to download a specific package (e.g., numpy), use:

pip download numpy -d ~/offline_pkgs

above command will download numpy with dependencies

docs.title: c. Transfer the Downloaded Files to the Offline System
docs.text:
Once you have downloaded all the required files, transfer them to the offline system. You can use scp, rsync, or a USB drive to copy the offline_pkgs directory.

For example:

scp -r ~/offline_pkgs user@offline-server:/tmp/

scp -r ~/offline_pkgs root@(ip addres or hostname):/tmp/

docs.title: a. Install Packages Using pip
docs.text:
Once the .whl files are transferred to the offline system, you can install them using pip.

Navigate to the directory where the .whl files are stored (e.g., /tmp/offline_pkgs).

cd /tmp/offline_pkgs

Install the packages using pip with the --no-index option to avoid looking for the packages online:

pip install --no-index --find-links=/tmp/offline_pkgs -r /tmp/requirements.txt

This will install the packages from the .whl files in the /tmp/offline_pkgs directory.

if you downloaded a specific package, you can install it directly:

pip install --no-index --find-links=/tmp/offline_pkgs numpy-*.whl

docs.title: b. Verify Installation
docs.text:
Once the packages are installed, you can verify the installation:

pip list | grep numpy

docs.title: Method 1: Offline Installation from Source (Tarballs)
docs.text: If you cannot use wheels for some packages, you can download the source code (tarballs) and build from source.

docs.title: Step 1: Download Source Code (Tarballs)
docs.text:
On an internet-connected machine:

pip download --no-binary :all: numpy

This will download the source code for numpy as a .tar.gz file.

docs.title: Step 2: Transfer and Build on the Offline Machine
docs.text:
Transfer the .tar.gz file to the offline system and install using:

pip install numpy-*.tar.gz

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
Proxy Network – Basics Guide

This guide explains what a proxy network is, why it is used, and how to use it, starting from the very basics. It is intended for students, developers, and anyone working in institutional or server environments.

docs.title: 1. What Is a Proxy?
docs.text: A proxy is an intermediate server between your computer and the internet.

docs.title: Normal Internet Connection
docs.text: Your Computer → Website

docs.title: Internet Connection Using a Proxy
docs.text:
Your Computer → Proxy Server → Website

Instead of connecting directly to a website, your request is first sent to the proxy server, which then communicates with the website on your behalf.

docs.title: 2. What Is a Proxy Network?
docs.text:
A proxy network is a setup where: - Multiple users access the internet - Through one or more proxy servers

The proxy server: - Receives requests from users - Forwards them to the internet - Receives responses - Sends the responses back to users

Proxy networks are commonly used in companies, universities, data centers, and HPC clusters.

docs.title: 3. Why Use a Proxy?
docs.text: Common reasons include:

docs.title: 1. Internet Access Control
docs.text:
• Restrict or allow access to specific websites
  • Widely used in offices, colleges, and research labs

docs.title: 2. Security
docs.text:
• Hides the user’s real IP address
  • Protects internal networks from direct exposure

docs.title: 3. Monitoring
docs.text: • Allows administrators to monitor internet usage

docs.title: 4. Caching
docs.text:
• Frequently accessed content loads faster
  • Reduces bandwidth usage

docs.title: HTTP Proxy
docs.text:
• Used for standard web traffic
  • Example: browsing normal websites

docs.title: HTTPS Proxy
docs.text:
• Used for encrypted web traffic
  • Required for secure websites

docs.title: 5. How a Proxy Works (Step by Step)
docs.text:
1. You request a website
  2. The request goes to the proxy server
  3. The proxy checks access permissions
  4. The proxy forwards the request to the website
  5. The website responds to the proxy
  6. The proxy sends the response back to you

docs.title: 6. Using a Proxy on Linux / macOS
docs.text:
Most command-line tools read proxy settings from environment variables.

Common variables: - http_proxy - https_proxy

docs.title: 7. What Does export Mean?
docs.text: In Linux/macOS: - export sets an environment variable - Makes it available to all programs started from that terminal session

docs.title: Example Commands
docs.text:
export http_proxy="http://username:password@proxy_ip:port/"
export https_proxy="https://username:password@proxy_ip:port/"

docs.title: Real Example
docs.text:
export http_proxy="http://application_user:Abc%60123456@100.100.100.100:100/"
export https_proxy="https://application_user:Abc%60123456@100.100.100.100:100/"

docs.title: 9. Breaking Down the Proxy URL
docs.text:
http://application_user:Abc%60123456@100.100.100.100:100/
Part Meaning http:// Proxy protocol application_user Proxy username Abc%60123456 Proxy password (URL-encoded) 100.100.100.100 Proxy server IP 100 Proxy port

docs.title: Note on URL Encoding
docs.text:
• %40 is URL encoding for @
  • Password Abc@123456 becomes Abc%60123456

docs.title: 10. What Happens After Exporting the Proxy?
docs.text:
Once exported:

  • Tools like curl, wget, pip, apt, and git
  • Automatically route traffic through the proxy

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
curl google.com
pip install numpy

docs.title: Temporary
docs.text:
• Works only for the current terminal session
  • Lost after closing the terminal

docs.title: Permanent
docs.text:
Add the export commands to:

  • ~/.bashrc
  • ~/.profile

docs.title: 12. Security Warning ⚠️
docs.text:
Proxy credentials are stored in plain text.

Recommendations:

  • Avoid sharing terminal screenshots
  • Clear shell history if required
  • Use secure credential management when possible

docs.title: 13. Installing Python Libraries Using pip Through a Proxy
Method 1: Proxy in the pip install Command (One-Time)
docs.text:
pip install pandas --proxy http://application_user:Abc%60123456@100.100.100.100:100

✅ Uses the proxy only for this command.

export https_proxy="https://application_user:Abc%60123456@100.100.100.100:100/"

Step 1: Create Config Directory
docs.text: mkdir -p ~/.pip

docs.title: Step 2: Create Config File
docs.text: nano ~/.pip/pip.conf

docs.title: Step 3: Add Configuration

[global]
proxy = http://application_user:Abc%60123456@100.100.100.100:100

docs.title: Step 4: Install Normally

pip install pandas  # ✅

If you see:

Connecting to 100.100.100.100:100

➡️ The proxy is being used.

Try:

  --trusted-host pypi.org \

docs.title: What is rpmbuild?
docs.text: rpmbuild is a Linux tool used to create RPM packages from source code.

docs.title: In simple words:
docs.text:
rpmbuild converts source code into .rpm files

These RPM files can then be installed, upgraded, or removed using standard package managers like:

  • dnf

docs.title: Why RPM Packages Are Used
docs.text:
On Rocky Linux, RHEL, and CentOS, software is managed using RPM packages.

RPM stands for Red Hat Package Manager.

RPM packages help to:

  • Install software easily
  • Track installed versions
  • Remove software cleanly
  • Upgrade software safely
  • Manage dependencies automatically

docs.title: Problems Without rpmbuild
docs.text:
If software is installed directly from source using:

./configure
make
make install

It creates several issues:

❌ No record of installed files

❌ Difficult to uninstall

❌ Hard to upgrade

❌ Not suitable for multiple systems

❌ No dependency tracking

This approach is not recommended for production or cluster environments.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
In RHEL-based systems like Rocky Linux, software distribution is done using RPM packages. The rpmbuild tool is used to convert source code into RPM files that follow system standards.

This document explains step by step how to:

  • Set up an RPM build environment
  • Build RPMs using rpmbuild
  • Understand build dependency failures
  • Successfully generate Slurm RPM packages

docs.title: Why it is needed
docs.text:
• Manual source installations are hard to manage
  • No clean uninstall or upgrade path
  • Difficult to deploy across multiple nodes

docs.title: Benefits of rpmbuild

• Standard package management
  • Clean install and uninstall
  • Version tracking
  • Easy cluster-wide deployment (HPC-friendly)

docs.title: Purpose

To prepare the system for building RPMs from source code.

dnf install rpm-build rpmdevtools gcc make autoconf automake libtool wget tar

docs.title: 4. Verify rpmbuild Installation
docs.text:
Ensure rpmbuild is installed and available.

rpm -qa | grep rpm-build

docs.text:
rpmbuild requires a standard directory layout to work correctly.

rpmdev-setuptree

docs.title: Created structure
docs.text:
~/rpmbuild/
├── BUILD
├── RPMS
├── SOURCES
├── SPECS
└── SRPMS

docs.title: 6. Download Slurm Source Code
docs.text:
RPM packages are always built from source archives.

wget https://download.schedmd.com/slurm/slurm-24.11.7.tar.bz2

Move the source archive to the SOURCES directory:

mv slurm-24.11.7.tar.bz2 ~/rpmbuild/SOURCES/

docs.title: 7. Extract Source Code
docs.text:
Verify the contents of the source archive before building.

cd ~/rpmbuild/SOURCES
tar xf slurm-24.11.7.tar.bz2
ls

docs.title: 8. Copy Slurm SPEC File
docs.text:
The SPEC file controls the entire RPM build process.

cp slurm-24.11.7/slurm.spec ~/rpmbuild/SPECS/

docs.title: 9. Run rpmbuild
docs.text:
cd ~/rpmbuild/SPECS
rpmbuild -ba slurm.spec

The build fails due to missing build dependencies.

docs.title: Why the Build Failed
docs.text:
rpmbuild checks the BuildRequires section in the SPEC file.

If required *-devel packages are missing:

  • The build stops immediately
  • This prevents creating broken RPMs

This behavior is expected and correct.

docs.title: Required packages
docs.text:
• mariadb-devel
  • munge-devel
  • pam-devel
  • readline-devel
dnf install mariadb-devel munge-devel pam-devel readline-devel

docs.title: 11. Run rpmbuild Again
docs.text: rpmbuild -ba slurm.spec

docs.title: What happens internally during rpmbuild
docs.text:
1. %prep – Unpacks source code
  2. %build – Compiles Slurm
  3. %install – Installs files into buildroot
  4. %files – Selects files for packaging
  5. RPM packages are generated

docs.title: Location
docs.text: ~/rpmbuild/RPMS/x86_64/

  • slurm-devel-24.11.7-1.el9.x86_64.rpm

docs.title: Final Summary
docs.text:
• rpmbuild is the standard RPM build tool for RHEL-based systems
  • It converts source code → RPM packages
  • SPEC file controls the entire process
  • Dependency checks ensure safe and reliable builds
  • This method is production-ready and HPC-friendly

docs.title: What is Hyper-Threading?
docs.text:
• Hyper-Threading (HT) is Intel’s implementation of Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT).
  • It allows one physical CPU core to appear as two logical cores to the operating system.
  • Each logical core can handle independent threads simultaneously.
  • Purpose: better utilization of CPU resources that would otherwise remain idle.

Analogy: Think of a chef (CPU core) who can cook one dish at a time. Normally, if the chef is waiting for water to boil (idle), nothing happens. With Hyper-Threading, the chef can start preparing a second dish while waiting — making the overall kitchen (CPU) more efficient.

docs.title: How it works (simplified)
docs.text:
• Each physical core has:
  • Execution units (ALUs, FPUs)
  • Cache memory
  • When one thread stalls (waiting for memory, I/O, etc.), the other thread can use the execution units.
  • The operating system sees twice as many cores, but performance does not double.

docs.title: Advantages of Hyper-Threading
docs.text: Advantage Explanation Better CPU utilization Idle execution units can be used by a second thread. Improved throughput More threads can run concurrently. Multi-tasking efficiency Useful for running multiple applications simultaneously. Cost-effective performance Acts like adding cores without buying more physical cores.

docs.title: Disadvantages / Limitations
docs.text: Disadvantage Explanation Performance not doubled Two threads share the same physical resources. Can increase latency Threads may compete for CPU resources. Security concerns Some side-channel attacks exploit HT (e.g., Spectre/Meltdown). Not always beneficial for HPC Certain HPC applications need dedicated cores for consistent performance.

docs.title: Hyper-Threading in HPC Environments
docs.text:
HPC workloads are compute-intensive and often parallelized using MPI/OpenMP. They usually:

  • Use floating-point-heavy calculations
  • Require predictable, consistent performance
  • Run on clusters with many nodes/cores

docs.title: Effect of Hyper-Threading in HPC
docs.text: Scenario Effect CPU-bound, floating-point heavy HT may not help; can slightly reduce performance because threads compete for execution units. Memory-bound workloads HT can help utilize idle CPU cycles while waiting for memory, giving small performance gains. Latency-sensitive applications HT can increase variability and slow down tight communication loops. Large MPI jobs Often better to disable HT for consistent core-to-core performance.

docs.title: General HPC Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Check your workload type
  2. CPU-intensive → HT off
  3. I/O or memory-bound → HT can be left on
  4. Benchmark your applications
  5. Run with HT enabled and disabled to see the effect.
  6. Cluster scheduling
  7. Schedulers (Slurm, PBS) treat logical cores differently.
  8. HT-enabled CPUs may require configuring threads per core carefully.
  9. Energy considerations
  10. HT may slightly increase power consumption.
  11. Security
  12. In multi-tenant environments, disabling HT can improve isolation.

docs.title: When to Enable / Disable HT
docs.text: Use Case Recommendation HPC scientific computing (CPU-heavy) Disable Hyper-Threading Multi-tasking / server virtualization Enable Hyper-Threading Mixed workloads Test & benchmark; enable only if performance improves

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• HT is not magic; it doesn’t double performance.
  • It’s good for throughput, not latency-critical HPC tasks.
  • In HPC clusters, most admins disable HT to ensure:
  • Predictable performance
  • Consistent benchmarking
  • Efficient resource scheduling

docs.title: Enable / Disable Hyper-Threading Manually (BIOS / iDRAC)
docs.text:
⚠️ IMPORTANT

  • The server will reboot
  • Ensure the node is isolated
  • Make sure no jobs are running

docs.title: Check Hyper-Threading Status
docs.text:
Run the following command:

lscpu | grep -E "Thread|Core|Socket"


### Interpretation

* **Thread(s) per core: 2** → Hyper-Threading is **enabled**
* **Thread(s) per core: 1** → Hyper-Threading is **disabled**

docs.title: Using nproc
docs.text:
If the server has 192 physical cores, run:

nproc
  • Output greater than 192 → Hyper-Threading is enabled
  • Output equal to 192 → Hyper-Threading is disabled

docs.title: Option 1: Network Access
docs.text:
If the server is accessible on the local network:

  • Access iDRAC using:

https://<server-ip> example: https://168.192.1.1

docs.title: Option 2: Direct USB Access
docs.text:
If the server is not reachable on the network:

  • Access the iDRAC console locally

docs.title: Steps to Enable / Disable Hyper-Threading
docs.text:
1. Log in to the iDRAC console
  2. Navigate to:

Configuration → BIOS → Processor Settings 3. Locate the following options:

  • Logical Processor
  • Virtualization Technology

docs.title: Configuration Meaning
docs.text:
• Logical Processor = Enabled → Hyper-Threading enabled

  • Logical Processor = Disabled → Hyper-Threading disabled

  • Save the changes

  • Reboot the server to apply the configuration

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• BIOS-level configuration is persistent
  • Recommended for production HPC environments
  • OS-level SMT changes are temporary and reset on reboot

docs.title: Lustre Server Installation Guide (EL9 / RHEL9)
docs.text: MGS + MDT using ldiskfs

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
• OS: RHEL 9 / Rocky Linux 9 / AlmaLinux 9
  • Architecture: x86_64
  • Lustre Version: 2.16.x
  • Filesystem Name: hpcfs
  • Target Disk: /dev/nvme0n2
  • Mount Point: /lustre01

docs.title: Step 1: Update System
docs.text:
dnf clean all
dnf update -y
reboot

docs.title: Step 2: Install Kernel Headers and Build Tools
docs.text:
Lustre kernel modules must match the running kernel.

dnf install -y \
  kernel-devel-$(uname -r) \
  kernel-headers-$(uname -r) \
  gcc make elfutils-libelf-devel

Verify:

uname -r
ls /usr/src/kernels/$(uname -r)

docs.title: Step 3: Install Lustre Repository
docs.text:
Use only one Lustre version (do not mix releases).

dnf install -y \
https://downloads.lustre.org/public/lustre/latest-release/el9/x86_64/lustre-release-2.16.0-1.el9.x86_64.rpm

Verify:

dnf repolist | grep lustre

docs.title: Step 4: Refresh DNF Metadata
docs.text:
dnf clean all
dnf makecache

docs.title: Step 5: Install Lustre Server Packages
docs.text:
dnf install -y \
  lustre \
  kmod-lustre-osd-ldiskfs \
  e2fsprogs \
  ldiskfsprogs

Verify modules:

rpm -qa | grep lustre

docs.title: Step 6: Load Lustre Kernel Module
docs.text:
modprobe lustre

Verify:

lsmod | grep lustre
dmesg | grep -i lustre

docs.title: Step 7: Remove ZFS (If Installed)
docs.text:
ZFS conflicts with ldiskfs.

rpm -qa | grep zfs
dnf remove -y zfs
reboot

After reboot:

modprobe lustre

docs.title: Step 8: Verify Block Device
docs.text:
⚠️ This step destroys all data on the device

lsblk
fdisk -l /dev/nvme0n2

docs.title: Step 9: Create Lustre Filesystem (MGS + MDT)
docs.text:
mkfs.lustre \
  --fsname=hpcfs \
  --mgs \
  --mdt \
  --index=0 \
  --reformat \
  /dev/nvme0n2

Expected output includes:

Target: hpcfs:MDT0000
Mount type: ldiskfs
(MDT MGS first_time)

docs.title: Step 10: Mount Lustre Filesystem
docs.text:
mkdir -p /lustre01
mount -t lustre /dev/nvme0n2 /lustre01

Verify:

df -Th | grep lustre

docs.title: Step 11: Validate Lustre Services
docs.text:
lctl dl
lctl status
lfs df

docs.title: Step 12: Configure Mount at Boot
docs.text:
Edit /etc/fstab:

/dev/nvme0n2  /lustre01  lustre  defaults,_netdev  0 0

Test:

umount /lustre01
mount -a

docs.title: Step 13: Final Validation
docs.text:
ls /lustre01
touch /lustre01/testfile
ls -l /lustre01

docs.title: Optional: Enable Cockpit
docs.text: systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket

docs.title: Verification Commands Reference
docs.text:
lsmod | grep lustre
lctl dl
lctl status
lfs df
dmesg | grep lustre

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Do not mix Lustre versions in repositories.
  • Kernel updates require reinstalling matching kmod-lustre.
  • Use separate devices for MDT and OSTs in production.

docs.title: What is query_other_jobs?
docs.text:
In PBS (Portable Batch System), the query_other_jobs option determines whether users can see the jobs that other users have submitted to the system.

  • Default Setting: True (Enabled by default)

Possible Values:

  • True — Users can see jobs submitted by other users.
  • False — Users can only see their own jobs.

docs.title: What Happens When query_other_jobs is Enabled (True)?
docs.text:
When query_other_jobs is set to True, users have the ability to view jobs that have been submitted by other users. This enhances transparency and coordination.

  • Job Visibility: All users can see each other's jobs.
  • Transparency: Users can check the status of any job on the system, even if they didn’t submit it.
  • Collaboration: It’s easier for users to coordinate and manage resources, especially in shared environments where multiple users are utilizing the same resources.

docs.title: What Happens When query_other_jobs is Disabled (False)?
docs.text:
When query_other_jobs is set to False, job visibility is limited to only the user's own jobs. This ensures privacy but limits transparency.

  • Job Visibility: Users can only see their own jobs, not those submitted by others.
  • Privacy: Job details are kept private between users, so no one can see what others are working on.
  • Limited Collaboration: Users can’t check the status of other users' jobs, making it harder to coordinate resources in a multi-user environment.

docs.title: How to Set query_other_jobs to False
docs.text:
To disable this feature, run the following command:

qmgr -c "set server query_other_jobs = False"

docs.title: When Should You Enable query_other_jobs?
docs.text:
You should enable query_other_jobs in environments where users need to:

  • Coordinate job statuses in a shared or collaborative environment.
  • Increase transparency so users can see each other’s job progress, helping to manage system resources more effectively.
  • Avoid conflicts by ensuring users know what jobs are running and if resources are being over-utilized.

docs.title: When Should You Disable query_other_jobs?
docs.text:
You should disable query_other_jobs when:

  • Privacy is a priority and you want to ensure that job details are only visible to the user who submitted them.
  • Security-sensitive systems where job-related information should not be shared between users.
  • Isolated environments where users don’t need to view the status of others’ jobs for coordination or resource management.

docs.title: What is LDAP?
docs.text:
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a protocol used to access and manage directory information services over a network.

A directory is a specialized database optimized for:

  • Read-heavy operations
  • Hierarchical data structure
  • Fast lookups

docs.title: What LDAP Can Do
docs.text:
LDAP is mainly used for:

  • Centralized authentication (users login across multiple systems)
  • Storing user and group information
  • Access control
  • Integration with services (SSSD, NFS, HPC schedulers)

In HPC environments:

  • Single user identity across login, compute, GPU nodes
  • Consistent UID/GID mapping
  • Centralized user management

docs.title: 2. LDAP Architecture
docs.text:
LDAP follows a tree structure called:

👉 DIT (Directory Information Tree)

Example:

dc=mycluster,dc=local
 ├── ou=People
 │    ├── uid=user1
 │    └── uid=user2
 └── ou=Group
      └── cn=hpcusers

docs.title: DN (Distinguished Name)
docs.text:
Full path to an object:

uid=user1,ou=People,dc=mycluster,dc=local

docs.title: DC (Domain Component)
docs.text:
Represents domain name:

dc=mycluster,dc=local

docs.title: OU (Organizational Unit)
docs.text:
Logical grouping:

ou=People
ou=Group

docs.title: CN (Common Name)
docs.text:
Name of object (group or general name):

cn=hpcusers

docs.title: UID
docs.text:
User login name:

uid=user1

docs.title: Required Packages

docs.text:
Create file:

vi root.ldif

dn: olcDatabase={2}mdb,cn=config
changetype: modify
replace: olcSuffix
olcSuffix: dc=mycluster,dc=local


dn: olcDatabase={2}mdb,cn=config
changetype: modify
replace: olcRootDN
olcRootDN: cn=admin,dc=mycluster,dc=local


dn: olcDatabase={2}mdb,cn=config
changetype: modify
replace: olcRootPW
olcRootPW: {SSHA}HASH

Apply:

ldapmodify -Y EXTERNAL -H ldapi:/// -f  root.ldif

docs.title: What is Schema?
docs.text:

  • Attributes

docs.title: Important Schemas
docs.text: Schema Purpose core Base schema cosine Extra attributes inetorgperson User objects

objectClass: top

o: mycluster

docs.title: What is TLS in LDAP?
docs.text: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is used to secure LDAP communication by encrypting data such as usernames and passwords.

docs.title: Why TLS is Required
docs.text:
• Prevents password exposure over network
  • Secures authentication
  • Required for production environments

docs.title: Types of Secure LDAP
docs.text: Type Port Description STARTTLS 389 Upgrades normal LDAP to secure LDAPS 636 Direct secure LDAP connection

docs.title: 1. Generate Certificate
docs.text:
mkdir -p /etc/openldap/certs
cd /etc/openldap/certs
openssl genrsa -out ldap.key 2048
openssl req -new -x509 -key ldap.key -out ldap.crt -days 365

Common Name (CN) must match server hostname (e.g., ldap.mycluster.local)

docs.title: 2. Set Permissions
docs.text:
chown ldap:ldap ldap.*
chmod 600 ldap.key

docs.title: 3. Configure LDAP for TLS
docs.text:
vi tls.ldif

dn: cn=config
changetype: modify
add: olcTLSCertificateFile
olcTLSCertificateFile: /etc/openldap/certs/ldap.crt
-
add: olcTLSCertificateKeyFile
olcTLSCertificateKeyFile: /etc/openldap/certs/ldap.key

ldapmodify -Y EXTERNAL -H ldapi:/// -f tls.ldif
