docs.title: Hardware Troubleshooting – HPC / Data Center Nodes
1. Identify Scope and Impact (Using OME)
docs.text: Before taking any action, clearly identify the scope and impact of the issue.

docs.title: Determine the Level of Impact
docs.text:
• Node-level issue
  • Rack-level issue
  • Cluster-level issue
  • Check whether running jobs are impacted

⚠️ Important: If jobs are running on the node, do not touch the node until jobs are completed.

docs.title: 2. Check Workload Manager Status (PBS Pro)
docs.text: First, verify node and job status from the scheduler.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
qstat -aw
pbsnodes -aSj | grep <node-hostname>

docs.title: What You Can Identify
docs.text:
• Node state (free, busy, offline)
  • Jobs running on the node
  • Job owner and job ID

docs.title: 3. Handling Nodes with Running Jobs
docs.text:
If the node is hosting any jobs:

  1. Do not troubleshoot immediately
  2. Wait until job completion
  3. Inform the respective users / higher authorities
  4. After job completion, proceed with troubleshooting

docs.title: Put Node in Offline Mode
docs.text:
pbsnodes -o <node-hostname> -C "hardware issue"

✔ This prevents new jobs from being scheduled on the node.

docs.title: 4. Check Cluster Health Status (Bright Cluster Manager)
docs.text: Use Bright Cluster Manager (BCM) to verify node health.

docs.title: Using cmsh
docs.text:
cmsh
device use <node-hostname>
status

Or:

cmsh
device list | grep <node-hostname>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Identify node health status
  • Detect cluster-wide issues

docs.title: 5. Centralized Hardware Alert Check (OME)
docs.text: OpenManage Enterprise (OME) acts as the single source of truth for Dell server hardware issues.

docs.title: OME Provides Alerts For
docs.text:
• CPU
  • DIMM (Memory)
  • PSU
  • FAN
  • Thermal warnings
  • Power supply redundancy
  • Firmware mismatches
  • Lifecycle controller logs

docs.title: 6. iDRAC Access for Node-Level Diagnosis
docs.text: Using OME, access the iDRAC console of the affected node.

docs.title: Using iDRAC, You Can Check
docs.text:
• PSU status
  • Fan status
  • Inlet temperature
  • Fan RPMs
  • Node-level patterns
  • Port status
  • Power consumption status
  • Sensor health
  • System event logs (SEL)

📌 Tip: If multiple nodes in the same rack show failures, immediately suspect:

  • Power issues
  • Cooling issues

docs.title: 7. Power Drain (Cold Power Reset) Procedure
docs.text: A power drain is recommended after identifying hardware issues.

docs.title: Best Practice
docs.text: Always collect logs first before performing a power drain.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Login to iDRAC console
  2. Navigate to Maintenance → SupportAssist
  3. Click Start Log Collection
  4. Save logs for analysis or Dell support

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Remove network cables

  2. PowerSync cable

  3. InfiniBand (IB) cable
  4. iDRAC cable
  5. Remove power cables from both PSUs
  6. Remove any additional power cables (if connected)

  7. Press and hold the power button for 2–5 minutes

  8. This drains residual power completely

docs.title: 10. Power-On and Recheck
docs.text:
1. Reconnect all cables
  2. Power ON the server
  3. Re-collect logs
  4. Observe iDRAC alerts
  5. If issue persists, raise a Dell support case with logs

docs.title: RAM Issue
docs.text:
• Pop-up error in iDRAC
  • Scenario 1: Remove faulty DIMM
  • Scenario 2: Swap DIMM position
  • Replace DIMM if issue persists

docs.title: InfiniBand (IB) Cable Issue
docs.text:
• Try a different cable
  • Perform power drain
  • If issue persists, replace IB cable

docs.title: PSU Issue
docs.text:
• Swap PSU positions
  • Check redundancy status
  • Replace PSU if issue persists

docs.title: iDRAC Access Issue
docs.text:
• Reset iDRAC
  • Check BIOS/iDRAC settings
  • Replace iDRAC card if required

docs.title: CPU Issue
docs.text:
• Boot server with 1 CPU / 1 RAM
  • Identify faulty CPU
  • Proceed with replacement

docs.title: Fan Issue
docs.text:
• Swap fan positions
  • If issue follows the fan → replace fan

docs.title: 12. Final Step – Node Recovery
docs.text:
Once the issue is resolved:

pbsnodes -r <node-hostname>

✔ Node is now available for scheduling jobs.

docs.title: 13. Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always check scheduler status first
  • Never disturb nodes with running jobs
  • Use OME as the authoritative source
  • Collect logs before power drain
  • Follow systematic isolation (swap & test)
  • Escalate to Dell support with logs if required

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document explains how to identify, confirm, and resolve DIMM (memory) errors using the iDRAC console, system logs, POST messages, and physical troubleshooting.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• iDRAC access
  • Console access (Virtual Console or Physical KVM)
  • Proper ESD precautions
  • Server powered safely

docs.title: Step 1: Identify the Issue in iDRAC Console
docs.text:
1. Log in to the iDRAC console.

  2. Navigate to:

  3. System Overview

  4. Hardware / Memory Section

  5. Check system health status:

  6. Look for Memory / DIMM warnings or critical alerts.

  7. Note:

  8. DIMM slot number (example: A1, B2, C1)

  9. Error description
  10. Timestamp of the error

Purpose: To confirm whether the issue is related to memory and identify the affected DIMM slot.

docs.title: Step 2: Collect Logs from iDRAC
docs.text:
1. From iDRAC, collect the following logs:

  2. Lifecycle Logs

  3. System Event Logs (SEL)
  4. Save the logs for reference.

  5. Verify:

  6. Any DIMM-related error entries

  7. Repeated or persistent memory errors

Purpose: Logs help confirm whether the error is intermittent or persistent and are required for escalation.

docs.title: Step 3: Perform Power Drain
docs.text:
1. Gracefully power off the server.
  2. Remove all power cables from the server.
  3. Presee the power on button Wait for 10 to 30 seconds (minimum).
  4. Reconnect the power cables.
  5. Power on the server.

Purpose: Power drain clears residual power and temporary hardware faults.

docs.title: Step 4: Observe POST Logs During Boot
docs.text:
1. Open the Virtual Console or connect to physical console.
  2. Power on the server.

  3. Carefully observe the POST screen:

  4. Memory initialization messages

  5. Any DIMM or memory-related errors

  6. If:

  7. Server fails to boot OR

  8. Any error appears during POST Then:
  9. Allow the server to complete power-up
  10. Wait 2 additional minutes
  11. Recheck logs in iDRAC

Purpose: POST messages give real-time confirmation of hardware issues.

docs.title: Step 5: Confirm DIMM Error
docs.text:
1. Compare:

  2. POST error messages

  3. iDRAC alerts
  4. System logs
  5. Confirm that the issue is specifically a DIMM error.

Purpose: Avoid unnecessary hardware replacement by confirming the root cause.

docs.title: Step 6: Power Off and Open the Server
docs.text:
1. Power off the server.
  2. Remove all power cables.
  3. Follow ESD safety guidelines.
  4. Open the system cover.

Purpose: Prepare for physical inspection of memory modules.

docs.title: Step 7: Verify and Reseat DIMMs
docs.text:
1. Locate the DIMM slot showing the error (example: A1).

  2. Check:

  3. DIMM is fully inserted

  4. Locking clips are properly engaged

  5. Reseat the DIMM:

  6. Remove the DIMM

  7. Reinsert it firmly into the same slot

  8. Verify all DIMMs:

  9. Properly seated

  10. Correct population order as per system guidelines

Purpose: Loose or improperly seated DIMMs are the most common cause of memory errors.

docs.title: Step 8: Power On and Observe Again
docs.text:
1. Close the system cover.
  2. Reconnect power cables.
  3. Power on the server.

  4. Observe:

  5. POST screen

  6. Any memory error messages
  7. Allow the server to boot fully.
  8. Check iDRAC logs and console.

Purpose: Confirm whether reseating resolved the issue.

docs.title: Step 9: Swap DIMM Positions (Isolation Test)
docs.text:
If the DIMM error still appears:

  1. Power off the server.
  2. Remove all power cables.
  3. Open the system.

  4. Move the DIMM to another slot:

  5. Example:

    • Original error: A1
    • Move DIMM from A1 → B1
    • Close the system cover.
    • Power on the server.
    • Observe:

  6. POST screen

  7. Console messages
  8. Wait until the server fully powers up.
  9. Check iDRAC logs again.

Purpose: To determine whether the issue is with the DIMM slot / motherboard.

docs.title: Case 1: Same DIMM Slot Shows Error Again
docs.text:
• Error remains on the same slot (example: A1)
  • DIMM moved, but slot still reports error

✅ Conclusion:

  • Slot or motherboard issue ➡️ Escalate to support / vendor team

docs.title: Case 2: Error Moves with the DIMM
docs.text:
• Error now appears in new slot (example: B1)
  • Error follows the DIMM

✅ Conclusion:

  • DIMM is faulty ➡️ Proceed with DIMM replacement

docs.title: Final Summary (Quick View)
docs.text:
• Identify error in iDRAC
  • Collect logs
  • Power drain (2 minutes)
  • Observe POST logs
  • Reseat DIMM
  • Swap DIMM positions

  • Decide:

  • Slot issue → Support team

  • DIMM issue → Replace DIMM

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
Enterprise servers are designed to operate continuously (24/7). However, hardware, firmware, or management-controller issues can occasionally cause the system to become partially or completely unresponsive.

In such cases, different levels of reset are available. A Power Drain is the most comprehensive reset method, ensuring that all residual electrical power is removed from the system and its components.

docs.title: 2. Why a Power Drain Is Needed
docs.text:
Even after shutting down or resetting a server, some components remain powered as long as the server is connected to power:

  • Management controllers (e.g., iDRAC )
  • NICs with Wake-on-LAN
  • PCIe devices
  • BMC and standby rails (5VSB)

These components do not fully reset during a normal reboot or hard reset.

A power drain clears:

  • Firmware lockups
  • Hung management controllers
  • Stuck sensors or fans
  • PCIe device initialization issues
  • Ghost hardware alerts
  • Unresponsive remote console or virtual media

docs.title: Level 1: Restart (Soft Reset)
docs.text:
What it does

  • Restarts the operating system
  • Hardware remains powered
  • Firmware state is preserved

Use when

  • OS is slow or unresponsive
  • Minor service or application issues
  • Planned maintenance

Risk

  • Minimal

docs.title: Level 2: Reset (Hard Reset)
docs.text:
What it does

  • Cuts main system power abruptly
  • Server reboots immediately
  • Standby power remains active

How

  • Press and hold power button for ~10 seconds

Use when

  • OS is completely hung
  • No response via console or remote management

Limitations

  • Management controller may remain frozen
  • Some PCIe or firmware states persist

docs.title: Level 3: Power Drain (Full Power Removal)
docs.text:
What it does

  • Removes all power, including standby voltage

  • Forces full reinitialization of:

  • Management controller

  • BIOS/UEFI
  • NIC firmware
  • PCIe devices
  • Power supply logic

This is the most effective recovery method.

docs.title: Step 1: Power Off the Server
docs.text:
• Use graceful shutdown if possible
  • If system is unresponsive, perform a hard reset

docs.title: Step 2: Disconnect All Power Cables
docs.text:
• Remove all PSU power cords
  • If redundant PSUs are present, disconnect both
  • Verify no LEDs remain ON

✅ This ensures no standby voltage remains.

docs.title: Step 3: Disconnect Network Cables
docs.text:
• Remove Ethernet / Fibre / management network cables

Why

  • Prevents wake signals
  • Ensures clean reset of NIC firmware
  • Avoids partial power via PoE

docs.title: Step 4: Drain Residual Power
docs.text:
• Press and hold the power button continuously for at least 10–15 seconds

What happens

  • Capacitors discharge
  • Remaining voltage on the motherboard is cleared
  • Firmware states are reset

🔧 Some vendors recommend holding the button for up to 30 seconds for stubborn issues.

docs.title: Step 5: Reconnect Power Cables
docs.text:
• Reinsert all PSU power cords securely
  • Confirm PSU LEDs show standby power

docs.title: Step 6: Reconnect Network Cables
docs.text: • Connect management and data network cables

docs.title: Step 7: Wait for Management Controller Initialization
docs.text:
• Do NOT power on immediately
  • Wait 2–3 minutes

Why

  • Management controller boots independently
  • Firmware initializes
  • Sensors and inventory are reloaded

⏳ Powering on too early can cause incomplete initialization.

docs.title: Step 8: Power On the Server
docs.text:
• Press the power button once
  • Observe POST sequence
  • Monitor system LEDs and fan behavior

docs.title: 5. Expected Behavior After Power Drain
docs.text:
After a successful power drain, you may observe:

  • Fans ramping up briefly (normal)
  • BIOS/UEFI reinitialization
  • Hardware inventory refresh
  • Management interface becoming responsive
  • Cleared false alerts or stuck errors

⚠️ First boot may take longer than usual.

docs.title: 6. When You Should Perform a Power Drain
docs.text:
Perform a power drain if:

  • Server does not respond to soft or hard reset
  • Remote management interface is unreachable
  • Virtual console does not open
  • Sensors show incorrect values
  • Fans stuck at 100%
  • PCIe cards not detected
  • Vendor support explicitly recommends it

docs.title: 7. When NOT to Perform a Power Drain
docs.text:
Avoid power drain if:

  • Server is running critical production workloads
  • Data is actively being written (risk of corruption)
  • Issue can be resolved with a soft restart

Always follow change-management procedures in production environments.

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text: ❌ Not disconnecting all power cables ❌ Powering on immediately without waiting ❌ Skipping the power-button discharge step ❌ Assuming a reboot equals a power drain ❌ Performing during peak production hours

docs.title: 9. Best Practices (Data Center SOP)
docs.text:
• Document before and after status
  • Notify stakeholders
  • Label cables if multiple connections exist
  • Monitor logs after recovery
  • Escalate to vendor support if issue persists

docs.title: What is a PSU?
docs.text:
A Power Supply Unit (PSU) gives power to the server. If the PSU fails, the server may not start or may shut down.

PSU error messages usually look like:

  • PSU0001
  • PSU0002
  • PSU0003

docs.title: Common PSU Problems
docs.text:
You may see:

  • Server not turning ON
  • Amber (orange) light on PSU
  • Power redundancy warning
  • No display (No POST)

docs.title: First checks
docs.text:
1. Make sure the power cable is connected tightly
  2. Check the power socket or PDU
  3. Press the server power button
  4. Check if any PSU warning is shown in iDRAC

docs.title: Step 1: Check Cables
docs.text:
• Remove and reconnect the power cable
  • Make sure PSU is fully inserted into the server

docs.title: Step 2: Swap the PSU
docs.text:
If the server has two PSUs:

  • Swap the PSU with the other slot
  • If the problem moves → PSU is bad
  • If the problem stays → board or motherboard issue

⚠️ Remove only one PSU at a time

docs.title: Step 3: Check PSU Type
docs.text:
• Both PSUs must be same model
  • Wattage must be enough for server hardware
  • After CPU/GPU upgrade, old PSU may not be enough

docs.title: Step 4: Check PSU LED Light
docs.text: LED Color Meaning Green PSU is working Blinking Green PSU firmware update Blinking Amber PSU problem No Light No power connected

docs.title: Replacing a PSU
docs.text: If the server has two PSUs (redundant), you do NOT need to shut down.

docs.title: Remove PSU
docs.text:
1. Unplug power cable
  2. Press release latch
  3. Pull PSU out slowly

docs.title: Insert New PSU
docs.text:
1. Slide new PSU into slot
  2. Connect power cable
  3. Wait a few seconds
  4. Check LED → should be green

docs.title: Important Safety Notes
docs.text:
• Never remove both PSUs at the same time
  • Use same type PSU only
  • PSU firmware update causes downtime

docs.title: If Problem Still Exists
docs.text:
• PSU may be failed
  • Or motherboard / power board issue
  • Contact technical support

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
✔ Check cables

✔ Check power source

✔ Swap PSU

✔ Check LED light

✔ Replace PSU if needed

docs.title: How to Replace the Processor in Dell PowerEdge R6625
Before You Begin
docs.text:
Before replacing the processor, make sure you follow these safety steps:

  • Shut down the server completely
  • Disconnect all power cables
  • Allow the server to cool down
  • Use proper electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection
  • Work on a clean and flat surface

docs.title: Tools Required
docs.text:
• Torx T20 screwdriver
  • Thermal paste
  • Anti-static wrist strap

docs.title: Basic Steps to Replace the Processor
Step 1: Power Off the Server
docs.text: Turn off the server and unplug all power cables from the system.

docs.title: Step 2: Remove the Server Cover
docs.text: Open the top cover of the server to access internal components.

docs.title: Step 3: Remove the Air Shroud
docs.text: Carefully lift and remove the air shroud to expose the processor area.

docs.title: Step 4: Remove the Heat Sink
docs.text: Loosen the screws on the heat sink and gently lift it off the processor.

docs.title: Step 5: Remove the Old Processor
docs.text:
• Unlock the processor socket using the release mechanism
  • Carefully lift the processor out without touching the pins

docs.title: Step 6: Install the New Processor
docs.text:
• Place the new processor into the socket correctly aligned
  • Lock it into position using the socket latch

docs.title: Step 7: Reinstall the Heat Sink
docs.text:
• Apply new thermal paste if required
  • Secure the heat sink back in place

docs.title: Step 8: Reassemble the Server
docs.text:
• Reinstall the air shroud
  • Close the server cover
  • Reconnect all power cables

docs.title: Step 9: Power On and Verify
docs.text: Turn on the server and check the BIOS to confirm that the new processor is detected correctly.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• Handle the processor carefully to avoid damage
  • Do not force any components into place
  • If an error appears on first boot, enter BIOS and confirm settings
